advantages.title: Five Strategic Advantages of Hydrogen Energy

topics.label: Zero Harmful Tailpipe Emissions
topics.takeaway: Clean operation begins at the fuel cell.
topics.body: Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity with water as the principal reaction product, producing no CO₂ at the vehicle tailpipe during operation.
topics.note: Tailpipe emissions and lifecycle emissions are different measures.

topics.label: Fast Refueling
topics.takeaway: Less downtime in suitable duty cycles.
topics.body: Hydrogen refueling can approach conventional fueling times in suitable vehicles, reducing downtime compared with some battery-charging scenarios.
topics.note: Actual duration depends on the vehicle, station and operating conditions.

topics.label: Cold-Weather and Heavy-Duty Capability
topics.takeaway: Match the powertrain to the mission.
topics.body: FCEVs can offer advantages in cold-region and heavy-duty operations such as long-haul freight, mines, and ports, depending on the vehicle design and duty cycle.
topics.note: Cold-weather performance depends on thermal management; the image illustrates mining use.

topics.label: Long-Duration Energy Storage
topics.takeaway: Connect renewable supply with later demand.
topics.body: Hydrogen can support multi-month or seasonal energy storage in appropriately designed systems, complementing batteries that are often optimized for shorter-duration storage.
topics.note: Storage duration, efficiency and economics depend on system design.

topics.label: Decarbonizing Hard-to-Abate Sectors
topics.takeaway: A pathway for selected industrial processes.
topics.body: Hydrogen offers a potential decarbonization pathway for selected steelmaking and chemical processes, long-haul heavy freight, and shipping where direct electrification may face technical or operational limits.
topics.note: Conceptual demand links; hydrogen is not always preferable to direct electrification.

barriers.title: Five Major Barriers to Hydrogen Commercialization

topics.label: High Total Cost
topics.takeaway: Fleet economics must work across the whole system.
topics.body: High vehicle acquisition and hydrogen costs challenge commercial fleet economics, with some projects still dependent on subsidies or policy support.
topics.note: Qualitative cost drivers; no numerical cost split is implied.

topics.label: Uneven Refueling Infrastructure
topics.takeaway: Vehicles and stations need coordinated investment.
topics.body: Refueling access remains uneven, particularly for passenger vehicles, creating a vehicle-and-station investment coordination problem.
topics.note: A conceptual feedback loop, not a map of station coverage.

topics.label: Low Share of Green Hydrogen
topics.takeaway: Production pathways shape the carbon outcome.
topics.body: Much of China's hydrogen production still relies on fossil-based pathways, particularly coal, limiting lifecycle carbon benefits unless production emissions are reduced.
topics.note: Upstream production emissions are distinct from fuel-cell tailpipe emissions.

topics.label: Limited Maintenance and Service Network
topics.takeaway: Service readiness is part of market readiness.
topics.body: Hydrogen passenger-vehicle servicing remains limited in some locations, including specialist maintenance capacity and replacement-parts availability.
topics.note: Illustrative service ecosystem; no nationwide coverage counts are asserted.

topics.label: Market Transition and Subsidy Dependence
topics.body: The briefing material indicates softer market conditions in parts of early 2026. The industry still faces the challenge of achieving competitive economics and sustainable business models with less subsidy dependence.
topics.note: Early-2026 observations; not full-year results or a forecast.
